newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Cyclone nears Australia's sugar, cotton belt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Cyclone nears Australia's sugar, cotton belt.

text.p: Cyclone Justin, building off the north Queensland coast, could provide needed rain to parched sugar cane fields in Australia but also threatens to damage cotton crops, growers and rural industry officials said on Monday.
John Desmarchelier, general manager of the Australian Sugar Milling Council, said experience indicated that cyclonic rain effects were beneficial for the sugar crop if intensity was not enormous.
The periphery of cyclone Justin could bring some rain to the Bundaberg region, which had been dry so far.

Justin was near-stationary about 500 km east of Cairns and 470 km north of the town of Bowen on Monday morning and not expected to reach the coast until a few days' time, the Bureau of Meteorology said.
Cyclones would cause some damage but, on balance, rain benefits could outweigh damage costs, he said.
Weather over much of Queensland had been favourable for growing so far this season except for dry conditions in the south, he said.
Cutting of the 1997 sugar cane crop would begin in May or June.
Cotton growers in Australia's main producing area, northern New South Wales, were not greatly concerned with the approach of cyclone Justin.
"The Lower Namoi Valley is a long way away," Matthew Berry, grower services manager for Namoi Cotton Co-operative, said.

But the buildup of the cyclone was "a genuine concern" in Queensland, which produces 30 to 40 percent of Australia's cotton crop. Queensland cotton was only two to three weeks from picking and at a vulnerable time if exposed to rain, he said.
It was too early to be more definite about possible effects, sugar and cotton industry spokesmen said.
The Port of Townsville, Queensland's busiest port, was on yellow alert, meaning it was monitoring the cyclone's whereabouts, a spokesman for the port said.
However, there were no ships currently in the port, he said.
